cells.tense: You are reading the shape of things as they stand, and the read stays open.
cells.act: feel it alongside them and keep your own side
cells.ask: When something sits wrong between you and another person, say what you notice once, plainly, then leave their half alone — you don't have to carry it for them.
cells.core:
You're in a place where things get weighed — who has what, who owes what, what's fair. And you can see the whole shape: the parts, how they fit, where the pressure sits. That's real reading, and it comes without hard corners. Whatever you land on is allowed to keep moving as you learn more, and staying like that is what holds this steady.

What keeps it working: when you read something in a shared situation, you can say it without picking up the other person's load along with it. State what you notice, once, and then leave their side of it where it is — no needing to feel it for them, no settling it for them. That's the difference between being connected to someone and running their half of it, and it's what keeps you good to have around.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the whole shape without closing it.
cells.place: where what's shared is weighed and rebalanced

cells.tense: You will read it clearly and then pass sentence before anyone can answer.
cells.act: choose this, not that, and mean it
cells.ask: Catch one judgment before it lands. Decide you don't need the verdict today — watch what the situation is doing, and pick your next move because you chose it.
cells.core:
You already read the whole shape. That's real, and trouble starts when the reading turns into a ruling — what's wrong with the arrangement, who can't be trusted, how it ought to be. From there it's a short step to reading a person off one pattern, and to being sure your version of it is the fair one. From where they stand it's a sentence, and it settles before anyone can answer.

One way back: take one verdict and hold it. Not lose the pattern — just don't use it to decide what someone is, only to decide what you do next. Pick your next move and mean it, from what's actually here and not from the pattern you've already built. The pattern stays. The gavel comes off the table.
cells.sheetLine: Reading it is real. The verdict is a choice.
cells.place: where what's shared is weighed and rebalanced

cells.tense: There was a pattern in front of you and you kept peering past it, waiting for daybreak.
cells.act: open the thing you have been assuming you knew and look at it unlabelled
cells.ask: Take a situation you're sure about. Look at it again with no name attached — just what's there — and keep the name only if it still earns the place.
cells.core:
There's a situation you've been circling — reading it, weighing it, waiting for the fair picture to arrive — and the search hasn't landed. You already have most of what it takes to see what's true here. What's gone slack is staying open long enough to notice; endless scanning with the answer sitting just at the edge, untouched. That's not blindness. It's not arriving at what you half see.

A way back in: take a thing you're sure you understand and look at it again with no label on it. Not to prove yourself wrong — just to let it be strange for a minute, the way it was before you decided. If the name still fits, you keep it, and now you've actually held it. If it doesn't, you've found where this was waiting to start.
cells.sheetLine: You keep scanning. The answer is already half in your hand.
cells.place: where what's shared is weighed and rebalanced

cells.tense: You are already reading the room, and the reading carries no name on it.
cells.act: put it in proportion, not in punishment
cells.ask: When things are out of balance between you and someone else, name the fair measure out loud before you act on it — then adjust only that far.
cells.core:
You read situations — where the weight is off, what's fair, what's owed. Here that's already running. You sense, in the moment, what the right adjustment would be, and often you make it. Ask about it and it comes out as just how things work, nothing to do with you. The reading is doing its job. Someone is steering it, and that hasn't been signed.

Next time you feel the imbalance between you and another person, say the fair measure out loud — to them if they're there, to yourself if not — before you move on it. Then adjust. A sentence, not a speech: this is what's owed, this is what's fair. Saying it puts you beside the act. From there both sides can move again, and the read gets a name on it.
cells.sheetLine: You already sense what's fair. Say it out loud.
cells.place: where what's shared is weighed and rebalanced

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: that the person's pattern-seeing in this seat is recognised by others as fair or unfair — the record says calibration, not their reputation, so I keep the reading on what the capacity does, not what people think of it. The reader could reasonably say they simply see clearly and the room agrees, and my read of an imbalance is wrong; the asks survive that because each is small and independently useful — a pause, a single choice, a slot moved. The sentence serving me more than them would be any line where I sound like I already know their history; I've cut the motive and left the description.
